```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(poolinfo.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
sci <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
# An upper bound in the text, rounded up so that it stays true.
sci_up <- function(x) {
  e <- floor(log10(x))
  formatC(ceiling(x / 10^e * 10 - 1e-9) / 10 * 10^e, format = "e", digits = 1)
}
# A number as the paper prints it, without the zero before the point.
as_printed <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sub("^(-?)0[.]", "\\1.", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits))
}
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
```

In this vignette we describe how poolinfo computes its posterior summaries
and what evidence there is that they are accurate. We begin with the
marginal posterior of the between-site standard deviation and the conditions
under which its moments exist, then describe the default quadrature rule and
the checks that come with every fit. Next come the second engine and how
the two engines compare, the tests' tolerances, and our
reproduction of the numbers in @lee2026. We end with the derivations behind
the parts of the package that go beyond the paper, and a table that maps the
paper's notation to the package's.

```{r library}
library(poolinfo)
```

## Integrating out the mean

Collect the site estimates $\hat\tau_1, \dots, \hat\tau_J$ in a vector $y$,
and let $X$ be the $J \times p$ design matrix of the mean model, with rows
$x_j^\top$. For a common mean it is a column of ones, and $p = 1$. Site
effects are normal around $x_j^\top\beta$ with standard deviation
$\sigma_\tau$, and the estimates are normal around the effects with known
variances $v_j$. Write $w_j = 1/(\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)$ and
$W = \mathrm{diag}(w_1, \dots, w_J)$, let $b = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y$
be the weighted least-squares fit, and let $Q = (y - Xb)^\top W (y - Xb)$ be
its weighted residual sum of squares. Under a flat prior on $\beta$,
integrating $\beta$ out of the likelihood leaves the posterior density of
$\sigma_\tau$, up to a constant,

$$
g(\sigma_\tau) = \pi(\sigma_\tau)\, |X^\top W X|^{-1/2}
\prod_j (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)^{-1/2} \exp(-Q/2),
$$

where $\pi$ is the prior density of $\sigma_\tau$. Apart from $\pi$, $g$ is
the restricted likelihood of a random-effects meta-regression at
$\tau^2 = \sigma_\tau^2$ in metafor's notation [@harville1974; @viechtbauer2010]. Under the
flat prior on $\sigma_\tau$, then, the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$
peaks at the REML estimate of $\sigma_\tau$. For a common mean,
$X^\top W X = \sum_j w_j$, $b$ is the precision-weighted mean, and $g$ is
equation (D.2) of @lee2026. Every diagnostic is a function of $\sigma_\tau$
and the $v_j$ alone, so each of its posterior summaries is a one-dimensional
integral against $g$.

## Tails and moments

For every $\sigma_\tau \ge B > 0$ we have three bounds, where $v_{\max}$ is
the largest $v_j$:

- $\exp(-Q/2) \le 1$,
- $\prod_j (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)^{-1/2} \le \sigma_\tau^{-J}$, and
- $X^\top W X \ge X^\top X / (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_{\max})$ in the matrix
  order.

Together they give

$$
g(\sigma_\tau) \le |X^\top X|^{-1/2} (1 + v_{\max}/B^2)^{p/2}\,
\sigma_\tau^{p - J}\, \pi(\sigma_\tau), \qquad \sigma_\tau \ge B,
$$

which for $p = 1$ is the tail bound of Appendix D.3 of the paper. In the
limit the bound is sharp. As $\sigma_\tau$ grows, $Q$ tends to 0 and the
ratio of $g(\sigma_\tau)$ to $\sigma_\tau^{p - J} \pi(\sigma_\tau)$ tends to
$|X^\top X|^{-1/2}$, so the tail of $g$ is that of
$\sigma_\tau^{p - J} \pi(\sigma_\tau)$.

Suppose the prior density falls off like $\sigma_\tau^{-k}$, with $k = 0$
for the flat prior, $k = \nu + 1$ for a half-t prior with $\nu$ degrees of
freedom and $k = 2$ for the half-Cauchy. Then the posterior mean of
$\sigma_\tau^q$ is finite exactly when $J > q + p + 1 - k$, and the case
$q = 0$ is the condition for a proper posterior. Under the half-normal and
uniform priors every moment exists. A flat prior thus needs $J \ge p + 2$
sites. A proper prior gives a proper posterior with as few as $p$ sites.
With $J = p$, however, the fitted values reproduce the estimates whatever
$\sigma_\tau$ is, $g$ is a constant times $\pi$, and the posterior is the
prior. For that reason the package asks for at least $p + 1$ sites under a
proper prior. It integrates only the moments that exist and reports the
others as not defined. A posterior mean of a mean-model coefficient
requires the first absolute moment of its marginal distribution. Since its
conditional standard deviation grows proportionally to $\sigma_\tau$, this
requires $E(\sigma_\tau)$ to exist: at least $p + 3$ sites under the flat
prior. Its standard deviation requires $E(\sigma_\tau^2)$, hence $p + 4$
sites. Central intervals remain available when these moments do not exist.

The upper end $B$ of the integrals is doubled until the bound on the
omitted tail of every moment that exists is within its limit, at most 400
times. A moment that exists can still need a larger $B$ than that when its
tail falls off very slowly: the mean of $\sigma_\tau$ with 2 sites and a
half-t prior with 0.05 degrees of freedom has a tail bound that falls like
$B^{-0.05}$. Both engines then stop with an error that names the moment.
A prior with a lighter tail avoids it.

## Quadrature on panels

The default engine, `posterior_control(engine = "nodes")`, builds one
quadrature rule in $\sigma_\tau$ for each fit and uses it for every summary
of the fit. Above a lower end $\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$ the rule is composite
Gauss-Legendre quadrature on $t = \log\sigma_\tau$, with the Jacobian
$d\sigma_\tau = \sigma_\tau\,dt$ in its weights. At the start no panel is
wider than 0.5 on the log scale. We halve a panel until its 16-point and
32-point rules agree, for the posterior mass and for the second moment when
it exists. They agree when they differ by less than $10^{-14}$ of the total
or $64J\epsilon$ of the panel's own integral, whichever is larger, where
$\epsilon$ is the machine epsilon. Below the second limit, the rounding
error of $\log g$, a sum of $J$ terms, no amount of halving brings the two
rules closer. Each panel of the final rule has 32 nodes.

Below $\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$ the rule is a single 32-point Gauss-Legendre
panel in $\sigma_\tau$ itself. Panels on the log scale cannot reach 0, yet
under every prior of `sd_prior()` the posterior density of $\sigma_\tau$ is
positive there, and roughly $g(0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$ of the
unnormalized mass lies between 0 and $\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$. We set
$\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$ to $e^{-8}$ times the smallest standard error, or
times the scale of a proper prior or the upper limit of a uniform prior if
that is smaller. Below it $\sigma_\tau^2$ is less than $e^{-16}$ times every
$v_j$, and neither the likelihood nor the prior changes much.

Under a uniform prior the upper end $B$ is the prior's upper limit.
Otherwise $B$ starts well beyond the spread of the estimates and the
standard errors, and is doubled until the bounds of the previous section,
divided by the mass below $B$, meet two limits. The bound on the mass must
fall below $10^{-12}$, and the bound on $E(\sigma_\tau^q)$ below
$10^{-10}\,\mathrm{GM}(v)^{q/2}$, for each of $q = 1, 2, 4$ whose moment
exists. Dividing by the mass below $B$ rather than the whole makes the
bounds conservative. With the factor $\mathrm{GM}(v)^{q/2}$ the limits
change with the units of the estimates, so the rule does not depend on them.
We compare the bounds with their limits on the log scale, where no power of
$\sigma_\tau$ overflows. Within a panel, the distribution function is the
integral of the Legendre series that matches the density at the panel's 32
nodes, and the quantiles are its roots.

We use the passing outcome of the credit recovery study as the example. Each
fit stores its rule as `fit$rule`.

```{r rule}
fit <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = ocrs)
rule <- fit$rule
data.frame(nodes = length(rule$sigma), panels = length(rule$edges) - 1,
           sigma_lo = rule$sigma_lo, B = rule$upper)
```

```{r rule-facts, include = FALSE}
n_panels <- length(rule$edges) - 1
gm_se <- exp(mean(log(ocrs$se)))
sigma_upper <- profile_summary(fit)$upper[profile_summary(fit)$quantity ==
                                             "sigma_tau"]
stopifnot(length(rule$sigma) == 32 * (n_panels + 1),
          sum(rule$panel == 0) == 32,
          abs(rule$sigma_lo - exp(-8) * min(ocrs$se)) < 1e-15)
if (has_metafor) {
  # The posterior density of sigma_tau peaks at the REML estimate.
  dens <- functional_density(fit, "sigma_tau", n = 4001)
  reml_ocrs <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = ocrs, method = "REML")
  step_grid <- diff(dens$value[1:2])
  stopifnot(abs(dens$value[which.max(dens$density)] - sqrt(reml_ocrs$tau2)) <
              2 * step_grid)
}
```

The rule has `r length(rule$sigma)` nodes, 32 in each of the `r n_panels`
panels above $\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}$, here `r sci(rule$sigma_lo)`, and 32
below it. Its upper end, $B = `r num(rule$upper)`$, is
`r round(rule$upper / gm_se)` times
$\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} = `r num(gm_se, 3)`$ and
`r round(rule$upper / sigma_upper)` times the 97.5% quantile of
$\sigma_\tau$.

## Numerical checks

Every fit carries checks of its integration, which `check_numerics()` lists.

```{r checks}
check_numerics(fit)[, c("check", "value", "limit", "status")]
```

```{r checks-facts, include = FALSE}
ch <- check_numerics(fit)
stopifnot(all(ch$status == "ok"), nrow(ch) == 9)
```

The first four rows compare the rule with two others. Halving every panel
tests whether the panels are fine enough, and moving the lower end down to
$\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}/2$ tests the treatment of the mass near 0. Each
compares the normalizing constants and the posterior means of $I$ and $H$,
as relative differences, with the limit $10^{-10}$, or $64J\epsilon$ if that
is larger. The next rows bound the mass beyond $B$ and, for the orders that
exist, the part of $E(\sigma_\tau^q)$ beyond $B$, divided by
$\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}^q$. The last row compares $H$'s turning point, on the
logit scale, as found by two scans of different resolution. For this fit the
largest relative difference between rules is `r sci(max(ch$value[1:4]))`,
and the tail bounds are at most `r sci_up(max(ch$value[5:8]))`. Since $B$ is
doubled only until the tail bounds pass, in other fits those rows can come
close to their limits. A value outside its limit makes
`reliability_posterior()` give a warning that points to `check_numerics()`.

## The adaptive engine

`posterior_control(engine = "adaptive")` computes each posterior mean,
probability and quantile as a separate integral with `stats::integrate()`,
as in the computation of @lee2026. On a finite range `integrate()` uses the
adaptive Gauss-Kronrod routine of QUADPACK [@piessens1983], which starts
from a single 21-point rule over the whole range. When the integrand is
concentrated in a small part of a long range, that first rule can miss it,
and `integrate()` returns 0 with an error estimate of 0:

```{r integrate-miss}
integrate(dnorm, 0, 1e4, mean = 60, sd = 0.5)
```

```{r integrate-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(integrate(dnorm, 0, 1e4, mean = 60, sd = 0.5)$value == 0,
          abs(integrate(dnorm, 0, 100, mean = 60, sd = 0.5)$value - 1) < 1e-8)
```

Its true value is 1. Splitting the range so that the peak falls in a piece
of moderate length avoids the failure. So the adaptive engine splits the
range at $\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}$, as the paper did, and also at 9 points
spread evenly on the log scale over the stretch where the density of
$\log\sigma_\tau$ exceeds $e^{-70}$ times its largest value. Besides these
extra splits, it differs from the paper's computation in two ways. Its
integrals end at the node rule's upper end $B$, while the paper's run to
infinity. And it takes the posterior standard deviations, and the intervals
of the site effects and of the coefficients, from a node rule. Each
integrand is scaled before it is integrated so that `integrate()`'s absolute
tolerance acts as a relative one. For the eight schools, the tests check
that multiplying the estimates and the standard errors by factors from
$10^{-100}$ to $10^{100}$ changes the posterior means of the diagnostics by
less than $10^{-9}$, relative, under both engines.

The two engines use the same kernel $g$, the same upper end $B$ with the
tail bounds that fix it, and the same formulas for the diagnostics. The
adaptive engine also takes its standard deviations from a node rule. So
their agreement checks the integration over $[0, B]$, by panels and
Legendre series on one side and by adaptive subdivision on the other. The
kernel and the formulas are checked against metafor's restricted
likelihood, against brute-force integrals, and against reference values
computed for @lee2026 with separate code that integrates to infinity. The
node rule is the default because it is faster: a single rule serves every
summary of a fit, while the adaptive engine integrates each summary, and
each site, separately.

## Tolerances

Below are the tolerances of the tests, kept in
`tests/testthat/helper-tolerances.R`. The first row is for identities of the
profile algebra, which are true in exact arithmetic. The others govern two
comparisons, with full-precision reference values computed for @lee2026 and
between the two engines. In the fourth row, $x$ is the value being compared.

| Quantity | Tolerance |
|:---|:---|
| identities of the profile algebra | $10^{-12}$ |
| $I$, $\bar S$, $H$, $S_j$ and probabilities | $10^{-9}$, absolute |
| $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | $10^{-9}$, relative |
| $\sigma_\tau$, the mean effect, site means and standard deviations | $10^{-9}\max\{\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}, \lvert x\rvert\}$ |
| $E(\sigma_\tau^2)$ and its quantiles | $10^{-8}$, relative |
| $I$ at $E(\sigma_\tau^2)$ | $10^{-8}$, absolute |
| normalizing constant | $10^{-10}$, relative |
| turning point of $H$ (logit scale) | $10^{-7}$ |

For $E(\sigma_\tau^2)$ the tolerance is looser, because the posterior tail
of $\sigma_\tau^2$ is heavy. With 5 sites under the flat prior, its variance
does not exist. Brute-force integrals are less accurate than either engine,
and the tests that compare with them use looser tolerances:

- $10^{-8}$ for posterior means under proper priors, and for the means and
  standard deviations of the site effects
- $10^{-7}$, relative, for $E(\sigma_\tau)$ when the prior's scale is far
  below the standard errors
- $10^{-6}$ for the conditional moments of the site effects under a mean
  model, against a joint normal computation
- $10^{-4}$ for the kernel of a mean model, against a two-dimensional
  integral over $\beta$

## Reproducing the paper

The data set `ocrs` has the inputs of the credit recovery study's 6 analyses
in @lee2026. They are course passing in all 32 sites, in the 13 Algebra 1
sites and in the 19 English 9 sites, passing with covariates, credits
earned, and passing as a log odds ratio. The first five are the rows of the
paper's Table 5 and Table G.1, and the last is the log-odds row of Table
G.2. We fit each with both engines.

```{r analyses}
algebra <- ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1"
analyses <- list(
  Pooled = fit,
  `Algebra 1` = reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se,
                                      data = ocrs[algebra, ]),
  `English 9` = reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se,
                                      data = ocrs[!algebra, ]),
  Adjusted = reliability_posterior(estimate_adjusted, se = se_adjusted,
                                   data = ocrs),
  Credits = reliability_posterior(estimate_credits, se = se_credits,
                                  data = ocrs),
  `Log odds` = reliability_posterior(log_odds_ratio, se = se_log_odds_ratio,
                                     data = ocrs)
)
adaptive <- lapply(analyses, update,
                   control = posterior_control(engine = "adaptive"))
```

We tabulate the node rule's posterior means and interval ends to four
decimals.

```{r paper-table}
tab <- as.data.frame(compare_profiles(.list = analyses))
cols <- c("I", "I_lower", "I_upper", "mean", "H", "H_lower", "H_upper",
          "J_eff")
cbind(tab["analysis"], round(tab[cols], 4))
```

```{r paper-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(length(analyses) == 6,
          identical(as.integer(tab$J), c(32L, 13L, 19L, 32L, 32L, 32L)))
# The values that the paper's Table 5 prints.
table5 <- list(
  I = c(.67, .63, .71, .65, .32), I_lower = c(.50, .29, .49, .47, .02),
  I_upper = c(.81, .87, .87, .80, .60), mean = c(.66, .63, .70, .64, .33),
  H = c(.025, .016, .028, .028, .028),
  H_lower = c(.019, .009, .018, .021, .003),
  H_upper = c(.029, .020, .034, .032, .038),
  J_eff = c(31.2, 12.7, 18.5, 31.0, 28.8)
)
digits5 <- c(I = 2, I_lower = 2, I_upper = 2, mean = 2, H = 3, H_lower = 3,
             H_upper = 3, J_eff = 1)
for (col in names(table5)) {
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(round(tab[[col]][1:5], digits5[[col]]),
                             table5[[col]])))
}
# Table G.1: the mean effect, sigma_tau with its interval, I at
# E(sigma_tau^2), Pr(I > 1/2) and V; and the log-odds row of Table G.2.
g1 <- t(vapply(analyses[1:5], function(f) {
  s <- profile_summary(f)
  at <- function(q, col) s[[col]][s$quantity == q]
  c(at("effect_mean", "mean"), at("sigma_tau", "mean"),
    at("sigma_tau", "lower"), at("sigma_tau", "upper"),
    plugin_gap(f)$at_mean_sigma2[1], prob_above(f), at("V", "mean"))
}, numeric(7)))
table_g1 <- cbind(c(-.130, -.081, -.163, -.117, -.124),
                  c(.188, .189, .203, .184, 2.807),
                  c(.127, .086, .122, .124, .610),
                  c(.266, .339, .318, .261, 4.949),
                  c(.691, .691, .740, .673, .353),
                  c(.973, .818, .972, .955, .114),
                  c(.237, .158, .282, .260, .313))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(round(g1, 3)), table_g1)))
lo <- analyses[["Log odds"]]
lo_tab <- tab[tab$analysis == "Log odds", ]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  round(c(lo_tab$I, lo_tab$I_lower, lo_tab$I_upper, prob_above(lo),
          lo_tab$H, lo_tab$V), 3),
  c(.530, .253, .743, .627, .035, .306))))
pooled <- tab[tab$analysis == "Pooled", ]
```

Rounded as the paper rounds them, the first five rows are the entries of its
Table 5, and the last row gives $I$ and $H$ in the log-odds row of its Table
G.2. The other numbers in the paper's Tables G.1 and G.2 for these analyses,
such as the posterior mean of $\sigma_\tau$, $I$ at $E(\sigma_\tau^2)$ and
Pr(I > 1/2), round to the paper's entries in the same way. Pooled passing,
for example, has $I = `r num(pooled$I, 4)`$ with the interval from
`r num(pooled$I_lower, 4)` to `r num(pooled$I_upper, 4)`, which Table 5
prints as `r as_printed(pooled$I)` [`r as_printed(pooled$I_lower)`,
`r as_printed(pooled$I_upper)`].

For each analysis we then find the largest difference between the two
engines over the posterior means and the ends of the intervals, in four
groups:

- the bounded diagnostics and the probability that $I$ exceeds 1/2
- $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$, relative to its value
- $\sigma_\tau$ and the mean effect, in units of $\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}$
- $\sigma_\tau^2$, relative to its value


```{r engine-differences}
differences <- function(a, b) {
  pa <- profile_summary(a)
  pb <- profile_summary(b)
  at <- function(p, q) unlist(p[p$quantity == q, c("mean", "lower", "upper")])
  gap <- function(q) abs(at(pa, q) - at(pb, q))
  rel <- function(q) abs(at(pa, q) / at(pb, q) - 1)
  c(bounded = max(gap("I"), gap("mean"), gap("H"),
                  abs(prob_above(a) - prob_above(b))),
    J_eff = max(rel("J_eff")),
    effect_scale = max(gap("sigma_tau"), gap("effect_mean")) /
      exp(mean(log(site_table(a)$se))),
    sigma_tau2 = max(rel("sigma_tau2")))
}
engines <- t(mapply(differences, analyses, adaptive))
signif(engines, 2)
```

```{r engine-facts, include = FALSE}
largest <- apply(engines, 2, max)
tolerance <- c(bounded = 1e-9, J_eff = 1e-9, effect_scale = 1e-9,
               sigma_tau2 = 1e-8)
orders <- floor(min(log10(tolerance / largest)))
stopifnot(all(largest < tolerance / 1000), orders >= 3)
```

Across the 6 analyses the engines differ by at most
`r sci_up(largest[["bounded"]])` on the bounded diagnostics,
`r sci_up(largest[["J_eff"]])` relative on $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$,
`r sci_up(largest[["effect_scale"]])` of $\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}$ on
$\sigma_\tau$ and the mean effect, and `r sci_up(largest[["sigma_tau2"]])`
relative on $\sigma_\tau^2$, at least `r orders` orders of magnitude inside
the tolerances.

The package's tests make the same fits and compare them, under both engines,
with full-precision reference values computed for @lee2026 and stored in
`tests/testthat/cases/ocrs-reference.rds`. For each analysis they compare 24
of the 28 stored summaries, including every number for these analyses that
the paper's tables print, within the tolerances above. In the same file,
`tests/testthat/test-posterior-reference.R`, they do this for 6 simulated
data sets whose reference values are stored in
`tests/testthat/cases/boundary-cases.rds`. Slower tests in
`tests/testthat/test-engines-slow.R` compare the engines on the 6 analyses
and on 500 random data sets of 3 to 200 sites. In these data sets the
sampling variances spread over several orders of magnitude, and about a
tenth of them have an outlying estimate. The slow tests also run the node
rule alone on 400 extreme data sets, with up to 10,000 sites and ratios of
sampling variances up to $10^8$, and require finite, ordered summaries and
every check within its limit. These tests take several minutes and run only
when the environment variable `POOLINFO_SLOW` is `"true"`. From the
package's source directory, this command runs them:

```sh
POOLINFO_SLOW=true Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "engines-slow")'
```

## Beyond the paper

The paper's computations are for a common mean and the flat prior. The
package goes beyond them in five places, and for each we give the derivation
and the tests that check it.

### Mean models

With $\beta$ integrated out, site $j$'s effect given $\sigma_\tau$ has
posterior mean $S_j\hat\tau_j + (1 - S_j)\,x_j^\top b$ and variance
$\sigma_\tau^2(1 - S_j) + (1 - S_j)^2\, x_j^\top (X^\top W X)^{-1} x_j$,
where $x_j^\top (X^\top W X)^{-1} x_j = h_{jj}/w_j$ and $h_{jj}$ is the
$j$th diagonal element of $W^{1/2}X$'s hat matrix. The tests compare $g$
with metafor's restricted likelihood for $p = 1, 2, 3$ and with a
two-dimensional brute-force integral over $\beta$. They also compare the
conditional moments of the site effects with a joint normal computation in
which $\beta$ has a very diffuse normal prior.

### Proper priors

The half-normal, half-t, half-Cauchy and uniform priors of `sd_prior()`
enter $g$ through $\pi(\sigma_\tau)$. The tail bound above contains
$\pi(\sigma_\tau)$, and the integral of the bound times $\sigma_\tau^q$
beyond $B$ has a closed form, or a closed-form bound, for each prior. It is
a power of $B$ for the flat and half-t priors, a normal tail probability or
an upper incomplete gamma function for the half-normal, and 0 for the
uniform prior, whose upper limit is $B$. We test the posteriors under each
prior against brute-force integrals, and each bound against the integral
that it bounds.

### Intervals for H

With the $v_j$ fixed, $\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j$,
so the centered logits $\Delta_j = \log\{\mathrm{GM}(v)/v_j\}$ do not depend
on $\sigma_\tau$, which acts only through
$m = \mathrm{logit}\, I = \log\{\sigma_\tau^2/\mathrm{GM}(v)\}$. Along this
path $dH/dm = \bar S - I$ [@lee2026, Proposition 2(i)], and differentiating
once more gives

$$
\frac{d^2 H}{dI^2} = -\frac{J^{-1}\sum_j (S_j - I)^2}{\{I(1 - I)\}^2},
$$

```{r concavity-facts, include = FALSE}
step <- 1e-4
path <- profile_path(fit, I = 0.4 + c(-step, 0, step))
second <- (path$H[3] - 2 * path$H[2] + path$H[1]) / step^2
S_04 <- site_reliability(se = ocrs$se, sigma_tau = path$sigma_tau[2])
stopifnot(abs(second + mean((S_04 - 0.4)^2) / (0.4 * 0.6)^2) < 1e-5)
```

which is negative unless all the $v_j$ are equal, and then $H$ and the gap
are 0 for every $\sigma_\tau$. With unequal sampling variances, $H$ is
therefore strictly concave in $I$ and has a single peak, where
$\bar S = I$. @lee2026 locates the peak by scans at two resolutions; since
there is only one, the package finds the single root of $\bar S - I$ and
keeps a scan as a check. For $0 < h < H_{\max}$
there are two values $\sigma_1(h) < \sigma_2(h)$ of $\sigma_\tau$ at which
$H = h$, and $H \le h$ if and only if $\sigma_\tau \le \sigma_1(h)$ or
$\sigma_\tau \ge \sigma_2(h)$. With $F$ the posterior distribution function
of $\sigma_\tau$,

$$
P(H \le h) = F\{\sigma_1(h)\} + 1 - F\{\sigma_2(h)\}.
$$

The package finds $\sigma_1(h)$ and $\sigma_2(h)$ by Newton's method in $m$,
kept inside a bracket by bisection, with the exact derivative $\bar S - I$,
and solves this equation for the quantiles of $H$. Near a constant profile,
or when $I$ is close to 1, $\bar S$ and $I$ agree in most of their digits,
and their plain difference loses those digits. To keep them, the package
uses the exact identity $S_j - I = -(1 - I)\, S_j\{\exp(-\Delta_j) - 1\}$,
evaluated with `expm1()`, and subtracts $I(1 - I)$ times the mean of the
computed $\Delta_j$, which rounding moves slightly away from 0.

### Draws from other software

The diagnostics depend on the draws only through $\sigma_\tau$, so draws of
$\sigma_\tau$ from any algorithm that targets the same model and prior give
the same posterior summaries, up to Monte Carlo error. `reliability_draws()`
computes their Monte Carlo standard errors with the effective sample sizes
of `posterior::ess_mean()` [@vehtari2021]. Its site summaries average over
the draws of the mean rather than integrate the mean out. In the tests,
draws from `profile_draws()` go to `reliability_draws()`, whose posterior
means must be within 4.5 Monte Carlo standard errors of the integrals.

You can compare a brms fit [@burkner2017] of the eight schools with the
integrals in the same way. In brms a standard deviation is bounded below at
0, so a Student t prior of class `sd` is the half-t of `sd_prior()`, and an
empty prior on the intercept makes the prior on the mean flat.

```{r brms, eval = FALSE}
library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(
  estimate | se(se) ~ 1 + (1 | school), data = eight_schools,
  prior = c(prior("", class = Intercept),
            prior(student_t(3, 0, 10), class = sd)),
  chains = 4, iter = 4000, seed = 1, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99)
)
from_brms <- reliability_draws(fit_brms)
from_brms
exact <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = school,
                               data = eight_schools,
                               prior = sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3))
exact
```

The posterior means that `from_brms` prints should differ from those of
`exact` by no more than a few of the Monte Carlo standard errors printed
beside them.

### Confidence intervals for the between-site variance

In metafor's notation $\sigma_\tau^2$ is $\tau^2$. Suppose an interval $C$
covers $\sigma_\tau^2$ with probability $1 - \alpha$. Because $I$ increases
with $\sigma_\tau^2$, the interval between $I$ at the ends of $C$ covers $I$
with the same probability, and so does the interval for $\bar S$. So does
the interval for $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ when the sampling variances differ;
when they are all equal, $J_{\mathrm{eff}} = J$ for every $\sigma_\tau$ and
its interval is the single value $J$. $H$ is not monotone, and `map_tau2_interval()` reports
its smallest and largest values over $C$ instead, using $H$'s peak when the
peak lies inside $C$. That range contains $H$ whenever $C$ contains
$\sigma_\tau^2$, so its coverage is at least $1 - \alpha$.

For a metafor fit, $C$ is the Q-profile interval of @viechtbauer2007 for
the model of the fit, moderators included. With $Q(\sigma_\tau^2)$ the
weighted residual sum of squares of the estimates at $\sigma_\tau^2$ (the
generalized $Q$ statistic), its lower end solves
$Q(\sigma_\tau^2) = \chi^2_{J-p,\,1-\alpha/2}$ and its upper end
$Q(\sigma_\tau^2) = \chi^2_{J-p,\,\alpha/2}$, where $\chi^2_{J-p,\,q}$ is
the $q$ quantile; an end is 0 when $Q(0)$ is already below its quantile.
`map_tau2_interval()` solves these equations itself, for
$\log(\sigma_\tau^2 / \mathrm{GM}(v))$, so that the ends do not depend on
the units of the effects and an end close to 0 has the same relative
precision as one far above it. It does so for every estimator of metafor,
also for `GENQ` and `GENQM` fits, whose own `confint()` uses another
method. The tests compare the mapped ends with the profiles
at the ends of the interval, and the upper end for $H$ with $H$'s peak when
the peak lies inside the interval. For the eight schools they also compare
the end found with that of `confint()` run with a wider limit. We fit the
eight schools with metafor and map its interval.

```{r tau2, eval = has_metafor}
reml <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = eight_schools,
                     method = "REML")
confint(reml)
mapped <- map_tau2_interval(reml)
attr(mapped, "interval")
mapped
```

```{r tau2-facts, include = FALSE, eval = has_metafor}
ci <- confint(reml)
end <- attr(mapped, "interval")[["upper"]]
gm_v8 <- exp(mean(log(eight_schools$se^2)))
I_at <- function(s2) s2 / (s2 + gm_v8)
stopifnot(identical(ci$ub.sign, ">"), ci$random["tau^2", "ci.ub"] == 100,
          end > 200, abs(mapped$upper[1] - I_at(end)) < 1e-12)
```

`r if (has_metafor) sprintf("metafor reports the upper end as above %s, and the interval that is mapped ends at %s. Through $I$ the difference is large, since $I$ is %s at %s and %s at %s.", format(ci$random["tau^2", "ci.ub"]), num(end, 1), num(I_at(100)), format(ci$random["tau^2", "ci.ub"]), num(I_at(end)), num(end, 1))`

## Notation

The paper and the package write some quantities differently. For each
quantity, the table below gives the paper's symbol, the package's symbol or
name, and the meaning.

| Paper | Package | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\hat\tau_j$, $v_j$ | $\hat\tau_j$, $v_j$, `estimate`, `se2` (`se`$^2$) | site estimate and sampling variance |
| $\sigma$, $a = \sigma^2$ | $\sigma_\tau$, $\sigma_\tau^2$, `sigma_tau`, `sigma_tau2` | between-site standard deviation and variance |
| $\tau$ | $\mu$, `effect_mean` | mean of the site effects |
| none | `effect`, a column of `site_table()` | posterior mean of a site's effect |
| none | $\beta$, `coef_*` | coefficients of the mean model |
| $\tilde v$ | $\mathrm{GM}(v)$ | geometric mean of the $v_j$ |
| $g(\sigma)$ | $g(\sigma_\tau)$ | unnormalized posterior density of the between-site standard deviation |
| $S_j$ | `reliability`, `site_reliability()` | site reliability |
| $I$ | `I`, `kl_centroid()` | informativeness |
| $\bar S$ | `mean` | mean reliability |
| $\mathrm{HM}(S)$ | `harmonic` | harmonic centroid |
| $H$ | `H`, `kl_dispersion()` | dispersion |
| $V$, $\rho_3$ | `V`, `rho3`, `logit_moments()` | logit variance and third absolute logit moment |
| $J_{\mathrm{eff}}$ | `J_eff`, `concentration_count()` | concentration count |
| $m$ | `logit_I`, a column of `profile_path()` | logit of $I$ |
| $\Delta_j$ | $\Delta_j$ | centered logits, $\mathrm{logit}\, S_j - m$ |
| $R_H$, $R_S$ | `exact` minus `leading`, columns of `local_terms()` | remainders of Proposition 2 |
| $\sqrt3\rho_3/108$, $\rho_3/48$ | `bound`, a column of `local_terms()` | bounds on $\lvert R_H\rvert$ and $\lvert R_S\rvert$ |
| $\kappa$, $n_j$ | $\kappa_j$, $n_j$, `kappa`, `n` | variance constant and site size, $v_j = \kappa_j/n_j$ |
